summary.text: The East Pacific Rise is a mid-ocean rise along the floor of the Pacific Ocean, on a boundary where tectonic plates move apart.
It is called a rise rather than a ridge because it spreads faster, which gives it less height and more regular terrain.
Near Easter Island its crust moves apart by more than 150 mm a year, the fastest rate in the world.

facts.label: Fastest spreading
facts.value: Over 150 mm a year near Easter Island

facts.label: Height
facts.value: About 1,800–2,700 m above the surrounding seafloor

facts.value: First discovered here by the RISE project, 1979

facts.value: Starts in the Gulf of California

items.prompt: Geologists call this Pacific feature a 'rise' instead of a 'ridge'. What is the reason?

options.label: It lies much deeper than other ridges
It has no volcanoes along it
It slowly sinks instead of growing
Faster spreading leaves it lower and smoother

items.explain: Its higher spreading rate produces less elevation and more regular terrain, so it is termed an oceanic rise.

items.prompt: A hiker climbs a volcano in the Andes. How is that volcano linked to the East Pacific Rise?

options.label: Plates moving east from the rise sink under South America
Magma flows sideways from the rise under the continent
The rise once ran right through the Andes
Heat from the rise warms the rock under the coast

items.explain: The Nazca and Cocos plates move east from the rise and are subducted under the American plates, and the Andes volcanoes are a direct result of that collision.

items.prompt: Creatures living at vents along the East Pacific Rise survive far from any sunlight. What powers their ecosystem?

options.label: Photosynthesis by deep-water algae
Chemosynthesis using chemicals from the vents
Food scraps drifting down from whales
Glowing bacteria that make their own light

items.explain: Vent creatures there live in a chemosynthetic ecosystem instead of one based on photosynthesis.

items.prompt: About 23 million years ago, the old Farallon plate sank under North America faster than new crust could replace it. What happened to it?

options.label: It welded onto the Pacific plate
It was pushed up into a mountain range
It broke into the Nazca and Cocos plates
It melted completely and disappeared

items.explain: Losing crust faster than it could regenerate, the Farallon plate split into two smaller plates, the Nazca and Cocos plates.

items.prompt: A survey ship maps a mid-ocean ridge and finds a deep, wide central rift valley along its crest. What does that suggest?

options.label: The ridge is spreading fast, like the East Pacific Rise
The ridge has stopped spreading entirely
The ridge is being pushed under a continent
The ridge is spreading slowly, unlike this rise

items.explain: Slow-spreading ridges typically have a deep, wide central rift valley, while the fast-spreading East Pacific Rise has a smooth, broad axial high.

items.prompt: Why might people looking for metal ores take an interest in the black smokers along this rise?

options.label: They are building up sulfide ore deposits
They spit out pure gold nuggets
They melt old ships into scrap metal
They pull iron out of passing whales

items.explain: These vents are forming volcanogenic massive sulfide ore deposits on the ocean floor.

paragraphs.heading: A rise, not a ridge
paragraphs.text: The East Pacific Rise is a mid-ocean rise on the floor of the Pacific Ocean, along a divergent plate boundary. It is called a rise rather than a ridge because it spreads faster, which leaves it less elevated and with more regular terrain. Much of it lies about 3,200 km off the coast of South America, standing some 1,800 to 2,700 m above the seafloor around it.

paragraphs.heading: Where it runs
paragraphs.text: The rise runs south from the Gulf of California to a point near 55°S 130°W. There it joins the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge, which heads west-south-west toward Antarctica. Along the way it divides the Pacific plate on its western side from the North American, Rivera, Cocos, Nazca and Antarctic plates.

paragraphs.heading: The fastest spreading
paragraphs.text: Ocean crust moves away from the rise on both sides. Near Easter Island it moves more than 150 mm a year, the fastest rate in the world, while at the northern end it moves only about 60 mm a year. Being a fast-spreading ridge, it has a smooth, broad, symmetric high along its axis, rather than the deep, wide central rift valley typical of slow-spreading ridges.

paragraphs.heading: Volcanoes on the far shore
paragraphs.text: On the eastern side, the Cocos and Nazca plates move east and meet the South American and North American plates moving west, sliding beneath them. This collision directly produces the chain of volcanoes in the Andes and the curving line of volcanoes across Mexico and Central America.

paragraphs.heading: Black smokers and vent life
paragraphs.text: The rise is a region of active, effusive volcanism. That underground heat drives hydrothermal activity, which gives many heat-loving species the temperatures, nutrients and protection they need. Hydrothermal vents known as black smokers were first discovered along the rise by the RISE project in 1979. These vents are building massive sulfide ore deposits on the ocean floor, and many unusual deep-water creatures live around them in an ecosystem based on chemosynthesis instead of photosynthesis.

paragraphs.heading: How it was born
paragraphs.text: The rise's history is tied to the ancient Farallon plate. About 30 million years ago, the Pacific–Farallon spreading ridge collided with the edge of North America, and the Farallon plate began to break apart. Around 23 million years ago, it was sinking under North America faster than it could be renewed, and it split into the Nazca and Cocos plates. After further reorganizations, including a major one about 2.5 million years ago, a new center of crust growth formed between the Pacific, Nazca and Cocos plates: the modern East Pacific Rise.
